query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A targeted, low‐temperature annealing treatment that induces an interfacial complexion transition will modify the chemistry and structure at the dual‐phase lamellar boundaries of the eutectic high‐entropy alloy, thereby reducing dislocation pile‐ups, alleviating local stress concentrations, and promoting more continuous dislocation flow during room‐temperature tensile loading. This intervention is expected to overcome brittle failure and enhance ductility, while retaining or even increasing the alloy’s high strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual‐phase lamellar microstructure exhibiting strong internal boundaries that act as obstacles to dislocation motion, leading to dislocation pile‐ups, local stress concentrations, microcracking, and brittle failure under tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Apply a targeted low‐temperature annealing treatment optimized to trigger an interfacial complexion transition (or controlled segregation) along the lamellar boundaries.
generation.conditions: Treatment and subsequent testing are performed under ambient (room-temperature) conditions, with the alloy subjected to standard tensile loading; the annealing temperature is chosen to be low enough to prevent coarsening of the lamellae while being sufficient to modify the interfacial chemistry.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified interfacial complexion at the lamellar boundaries characterized by segregated solute species and a reduced interfacial barrier, which facilitates easier dislocation transmission.
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment alters the interfacial structure and chemistry, lowering the energy barriers for dislocation motion across lamellar interfaces. This reduces the accumulation of dislocations at these boundaries, thereby diminishing local stress concentrations and preventing microcrack initiation while maintaining the fine-scale architecture that contributes to high strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the treated alloy will exhibit significantly higher room-temperature tensile ductility and reduced brittleness, with strength being maintained or modestly improved due to the preserved lamellar architecture.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic high‐entropy alloy with dual‐phase lamellar colonies that shows limited tensile ductility and brittle failure due to dislocation pile-ups at internal interfaces.
generation.boundary: The annealing treatment must be carefully controlled to avoid excessive diffusion or coarsening of the lamellar structure; benefits are expected only within an optimized regime of low-temperature and limited duration that specifically promotes an interfacial complexion transition without altering the bulk microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvements in ductility and strength retention is uncertain and may depend on precise annealing parameters and alloy composition. Optimization of temperature and duration is critical, and the response may vary with minor compositional changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of eutectic HEA samples and subject them to a range of low-temperature annealing treatments with varying temperatures and durations. Characterize the interfacial microstructure using high-resolution TEM and atom probe tomography to detect the formation of complexion transitions or solute segregation along the lamellar boundaries. Subsequently, perform standardized room-temperature tensile tests to assess ductility and strength. Compare the results with those from untreated samples.
measurements: Interfacial microstructure (TEM, APT) to verify complexion transition
Dislocation behavior during tensile deformation (in-situ TEM if feasible)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealing treatment fails to produce measurable interfacial complexion changes or if there is no statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility (or if strength is reduced) compared to untreated samples under the same room-temperature testing conditions, then the hypothesis that the tailored interface engineering via low-temperature annealing improves both ductility and strength is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), or multi-principal-element alloys, emerge as a new research frontier in the metallic materials community [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] . HEAs differentiate with conventional alloys in th

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. frame.system: A eutectic high‐entropy alloy characterized by a hierarchical microstructure with dual‐phase lamellar colonies, where the microstructural state exhibits internal boundaries that accumulate dislocations.
frame.goal: Improve room-temperature tensile ductility and reduce brittleness while retaining or even increasing the alloy’s strength.
frame.limitation: Limited ductility and brittleness under room-temperature tensile loading due to dislocation pile-ups at internal interfaces, which result in local stress concentrations, microcracking, and ultimately catastrophic failure.
constraints: A single intervention must be applied
The intervention should overcome brittleness while retaining or increasing alloy strength
Improvements must be realized under room-temperature conditions
frame.regime: Room-temperature tensile testing and ambient operating conditions, where the alloy is subject to conventional mechanical loading.
prior_attempts: Previous microstructural engineering approaches (e.g., phase refinement and multi‐step heat treatments) have attempted to modify lamellar spacing or colony size but have fallen short of simultaneously improving ductility and maintaining strength.
Efforts that addressed only dislocation mobility without altering the interfacial chemistry did not mitigate the localized stress concentrations effectively.

decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high‐entropy alloys (as in PMC4145285) has demonstrated that a fine dual‐phase lamellar architecture can yield high strength and reasonable ductility, yet further processing (e.g., cold rolling or multi‐step heat treatments) has been applied mainly to refine phases or enhance dislocation mobility. Subsequent studies then tried to alter bulk phase distributions or control secondary precipitations to improve ductility, but they largely left the internal lamellar boundaries untouched. In consequence, the core issue – dislocation pile-ups at these interfaces producing local stress concentrations and ensuing microcracking – has largely persisted.
decision.unsolved: The open challenge is how to modify the internal lamellar interfaces so that they no longer act as strong obstacles to dislocation motion. In other words, it remains unsolved how to engineer the interface chemistry/structure to ease dislocation transmission while retaining the fine-scale architecture that underpins the alloy’s high strength.
decision.lever: a targeted, low‐temperature annealing treatment designed to induce an interfacial complexion transition (or controlled segregation) at the lamellar boundaries
decision.why: This approach directly targets the mechanism underlying catastrophic damage—dislocation pile-up at the internal interfaces—by altering the interfacial chemistry and structure to lower barrier strength and promote more continuous dislocation flow. By tuning annealing temperature and duration to trigger a transition at the interfaces (without changing the overall lamellar architecture), both ductility and strength could be improved. This lever follows naturally from the trend of moving from bulk microstructural refinements to more precise interfacial engineering, in light of the specific failure cues provided.
